articles.title: In Moldova, teens are learning about democracy and elections through an app
paragraphs: This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Moldova is a relatively small post-Soviet state with a population of three million people. A landlocked country, it has a long border with war-torn Ukraine and Romania; with the latter, it shares the same official language . The territory that is now Moldova was once part of the Russian Empire, and later the Soviet Union, and Russia has been meddling in its affairs.

Moldova has a large Russian-speaking population and a problematic unrecognized territory: Transnistria, which is basically controlled by Russia. It also has European aspirations and was officially named a candidate to join the European Union in 2022, after Russia invaded neighbouring Ukraine.

The country’s most recent parliamentary elections were held in September 2025, and despite the record influx of Russian disinformation and other meddling, elections were recognized as fair and democratic by the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OCSE) observers . The pro-European Party of Action and Solidarity (PAS) won the elections with a small majority.

The initiative supported by Digital Spark is an app called VotEDU, which answers basic questions about the democratic institution of elections for high school students in Moldova. It does so through short, interactive lessons using quizzes, flashcards, and other easily accessible formats in three languages: Romanian, Russian, and English, and is the subject of this Spotlight story.
Global Voices interviewed the app’s developer, Vlad Garbuz, about the impact of Digital Spark and his initiative.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project.

Vlad Garbuz (VG) : I started VotEDU, an independent civic-education project in Moldova, to help young people understand democracy before they vote for the first time. The idea began at the VOTech hackathon in Moldova. I joined Digital Spark because I wanted to turn it into a tool that students could use in everyday life and teachers could bring into class. The project helped me build the app and begin testing it with the young people it is meant for.
GV : What issue or challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

VG : Young people meet politics every day through their feeds, long before they enter a polling station. In Moldova, many young people encounter misleading claims online. Yet many have very few easy ways of asking questions about elections and getting the answers they can understand.

That made me wonder how civic education could reach young people in the spaces where they already spend their time. VotEDU was the answer. It puts short lessons, simple explanations, and activities on their phones, so they can learn at their own pace.
GV : What are the key changes or activities that you implemented during your participation in the project?

VG : During Digital Spark, VotEDU developed into a civic-education app with nine units, 28 short lessons, quizzes, interactive activities, and a glossary of 136 civic terms. The content is available in Romanian, Russian, and English. All of the lessons have been reviewed for accuracy and political neutrality. Student privacy guided the app’s design. A short guide was also prepared for teachers.

VotEDU was represented at Moldova Digital Summit 2026, where several educators expressed interest in trying it in schools. The app is now being piloted with high school students in Moldova through its web version. It is also available on the App Store, with the Google Play version coming soon.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your beneficiaries and the community you serve? Please provide examples.
VG: Teacher feedback has highlighted the need for digital tools alongside Moldova’s electoral education textbook. VotEDU brings these topics into a format students can explore on their phones.

High school students in the pilot program are using the app and sharing feedback. The feedback tells us how easy the information was to access, as well as appreciation of the app’s design, quizzes, and illustrations. Together with teachers’ suggestions, this feedback is helping improve the content in the app and making it a better user experience.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed?

VG : I have learned that the design of a civic tool is part of its message. If an app is hard to understand, available in only one language, or careless with privacy, it may leave out the very people it hopes to reach.

Building VotEDU has made me more careful about how I explain civic topics. Each lesson needs to be accurate and fair, while still being simple enough to use on a phone. I now think more about whether young people feel comfortable asking questions and forming their own views, not just whether the information is online.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?
VG: The lesson I will carry forward is to start earlier. Young people should have a chance to understand democracy before an election campaign is asking for their attention.

I have also learned that a good idea needs to be tested with the people it is meant to help. Building VotEDU was only one part of the work. Now students are using it and telling us what they think. Their experience will help us see what works, what is still unclear to students, and what needs to change.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built?

VG: I will continue the pilot program and use feedback from students and teachers to improve VotEDU. I plan to bring it to more schools, including rural schools, and use short questions before and after the lessons to see what students learn.

In October 2026, I also demonstrated VotEDU at MEGAPHONE & e-Society in Skopje . I showed how digital tools can make civic education more useful and engaging for young people, and inspire others to try similar ideas. VotEDU is a project that can be adapted for different countries and topics. Making the project public and accessible is one of my objectives to ensure anyone can easily build something that will bring benefits to their local community.

articles.title: Support Global Voices’ January Spotlight: Independent journalism
paragraphs: Donate to our Independent Journalism Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!

Journalism has been a vital part of society for centuries. Writing about what happened and sharing it with others; reading about what happened somewhere else and discussing it with those around you; having a platform for letters, comments, and opinion about everything from the niche to the rich. Journalism has toppled governments and CEOs, revealed complicated scams, brought out the beauty of ethnographically observed daily life, recorded our qualms and foibles for posterity, and whipped up outrage, empathy, and triumph.

But journalism is on a precipice. The shift from print to digital has opened up new possibilities, as well as vulnerabilities. Changes in how we interact, especially at a distance, have changed what (and how) people want to read, listen to, or watch to understand the news.

This decade has seen dramatic changes in the field, from the loss of foundational trust in the institution, to digital, legal, and physical threats to journalists to the near-complete erosion of financial security for people who carry out this work. Increasingly authoritarian governments turn on the media, and the press in countries from Hong Kong to Myanmar to Russia to Nicaragua has been forced into exile .

Even countries such as the UK and the US have seen government targeting of journalists for critical reporting. Israel’s genocide in Gaza has laid bare the hypocrisy of the international press establishment, causing a crisis of confidence, while small local news outlets and independent journalists continue to report despite this.

Through it all, journalists have kept documenting, analyzing, responding, and reporting, even when they are underpaid and overworked, face hostile governments and terrible technology, sometimes from exile, in terrible conditions, even at risk of their lives. As we begin 2027, Global Voices will turn the spotlight onto these voices that continue to speak truth to power and bring to light the news that we all need to know. We will look at civic journalism, find out what is changing, and meet some of these indefatigable defenders of our right to free speech and our right to information.

articles.title: Bloody, brutal and growing: More states are adopting the firing squad as an execution method
paragraphs: The U.S. Army is scheduled to execute Nidal Hasan on Dec. 3, 2026, after Hasan killed 12 soldiers and one civilian at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth got President Donald Trump’s approval to use the firing squad to put Hasan to death .

However, the U.S. military hasn’t used the firing squad since 1945 . And the execution method has been minimally used outside the military, accounting for only six of 1,664 executions in the U.S. in the past 50 years. Since 1976, the firing squad has been used in only two states : South Carolina and Utah.

The infrequency of its use might seem surprising to many Americans. After all, the firing squad is the least complicated execution method ever used in the U.S. All that is needed are guns, bullets and marksmen.

Still, it has not caught on throughout America’s history. And as a scholar of execution methods, I know why. Firing squad executions are bloody and brutal, and the U.S. has been more comfortable using methods that appear more humane.

The first use of a firing squad in what eventually became the U.S. occurred in 1608 in the English settlement of Jamestown. George Kendal, a British naval officer, was tried, convicted and sentenced to death for mutiny and treason . He was shot rather than hanged because of his high social standing. It was thought of as a more honorable way to die.

In 1996, a group of archaeologists found the skeleton of a young man in the walls of the original Jamestown fort, in what is modern-day Virginia. The skeleton showed signs of several gunshot wounds, and the archaeologists suspected it was Kendall’s remains.
The firing squad was used in the American Revolution to punish desertion. During the Civil War, both sides used it to create a “public spectacle, a vision of terror” to discourage desertion.

The U.S. Supreme Court in 1878 upheld the constitutionality of firing squad executions . Firing squads, the court decided, would not bring the sort of “terror, pain and disgrace” that would violate the Eighth Amendment’s ban on cruel and unusual punishment .

Nonetheless, after the Civil War and into the early 20th century, the firing squad was used only in Utah and Nevada . In 1913, Nevada built a device that fired three guns by pulling strings. The move came after the state had trouble finding volunteers to serve on firing squads.

In 1915, labor activist Joe Hill was put to death in Utah by firing squad after being convicted of murdering three people. Hill had been a very vocal critic of capitalism and what he called the “greedy master class.” Some of his sympathizers claimed he was murdered as much for his activism as for his crimes.

As The Salt Lake Tribune noted in 2015, “Joe Hill was tied to a chair. Blindfolded. A small target was pinned to his chest. ‘Let it go, fire,’ he yelled. Rifles protruding from the blacksmith shop at Utah’s state prison obliged. Three of the bullets pierced his heart. The fourth went a little wide.”

In 1951, a firing squad execution in Utah went awry when the state put Eliseo J. Mares to death. He had been sentenced for the 1946 murder of an Ohio sailor who was killed while traveling to California for his marriage. Two of the four bullets missed Mares’s heart . They hit his hip and abdomen. He did not die quickly.

In January 1977, Utah also killed Gary Gilmore by firing squad . Utah law allowed prisoners to choose hanging or firing squad as execution methods. Gilmore elected the latter, saying it would allow him to “die with dignity.”
Gilmore was the first person executed in the U.S. after the Supreme Court‘s 1976 ruling that the death penalty was not a cruel and unusual punishment .

As Time magazine reported, “His neck, waist, wrists and feet were loosely bound to the chair. Twenty-six feet away hung a sailcloth partition with five slits. Hidden behind the curtain stood five riflemen armed with .30-.30 deer rifles, four loaded with steel-jacketed shells, the fifth with a blank.”
I believe the firing squad has not played a large role in America’s death penalty history because it’s offensive to this country’s evolving standards of decency.

As an anesthesiologist told The Associated Press in March 2023, “Inmates could remain conscious for up to 10 seconds after being shot depending on where bullets strike … and those seconds could be ‘severely painful, especially related to shattering of bone and damage to the spinal cord.’”
States abandoned the firing squad because it was thought to mimic the violence to which executions were responding .

But Hasan’s execution comes at a time of revived interest in firing squads as an execution method, aided by continuing problems with lethal injection . They are now legal in five states : Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah.
Idaho is the only state that designates the firing squad as its primary execution method. Idaho state Rep. Bruce Skaug has called the method “certain” and “quick.”
Others agree. In a 2017 opinion, Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote, “In addition to being near instant, death by shooting may also be comparatively painless.”

And in October 2026, former federal appellate judge Alex Kozinski applauded Hegseth’s decision to execute Hasan by firing squad. He was reiterating a view he expressed in a 2014 dissenting opinion: “Eight or ten large-caliber rifle bullets fired at close range can inflict massive damage, causing instant death every time.”

“Sure,” Kozinski added, “firing squads can be messy, but if we are willing to carry out executions, we should not shield ourselves from the reality that we are shedding human blood. If we, as a society, cannot stomach the splatter from an execution carried out by firing squad, then we shouldn’t be carrying out executions at all.”
On Dec. 3, Americans will again have a chance to consider whether they can stomach an execution by firing squad or whether they should be carrying out executions at all.

articles.title: Court of Arbitration for Sport
paragraphs: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS; French: Tribunal arbitral du sport, TAS) is an international body established in 1984 by the International Olympic Committee to settle disputes related to sport through arbitration. Its headquarters are in Lausanne, Switzerland, and its courts are located in New York City, Sydney, and Lausanne. Temporary courts are established in current Olympic host cities.

The International Council of Arbitration for Sport (ICAS) was established simultaneously, and a single president presides over both bodies. The ICAS, which has a membership of 20 individuals, is responsible for the financing of and financial reporting by the CAS, and it appoints the Director-General of the CAS.

Generally speaking, a dispute may be submitted to the CAS only if an arbitration agreement between the parties specifies recourse to the CAS. However, according to rule 61 of the Olympic Charter, all disputes in connection with the Olympic Games can only be submitted to CAS, and all Olympic international federations (IF) have recognised the jurisdiction of CAS for at least some disputes.

Through compliance with the 2009 World Anti-Doping Code, all signatories, including all Olympic international federations and National Olympic Committees, have recognised the jurisdiction of CAS for anti-doping rule violations. Starting in 2016, an anti-doping division of CAS judges, who specialize in doping cases at the Olympic Games, replaced the IOC disciplinary commission. These decisions can be appealed to CAS's ad hoc court in the Olympic host city or, if the ad hoc court is no longer available, to the permanent CAS. The inaugural anti-doping division handled eight cases, of which seven were doping cases within its jurisdiction.

As a Swiss arbitration organization, decisions of the CAS can be appealed to the Federal Supreme Court of Switzerland. Appeals of arbitration decisions are generally not successful, and no evaluation of the merits takes place, with the evaluation mainly based on whether procedural requirements have been met, and whether the award is incompatible with public policy. As of March 2012, there have been seven successful appeals. Six of the upheld appeals were procedural in nature. Overruling a CAS decision on the case's merits is extremely rare. It occurred in 2012 for the first time in more than 20 years when the Federal Supreme Court overturned the case of Matuzalém, a Brazilian football player accused of breach of contract. In 2020, the Supreme Court overturned the case of Sun Yang, a Chinese swimmer accused of doping. CAS decisions can be the subject of further appeal to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR). In Mutu and Pechstein v. Switzerland (2 October 2018), brought by the Romanian footballer Adrian Mutu and the German speed skater Claudia Pechstein, the ECHR found no violation of Article 6(1) of the Convention regarding the independence and impartiality of CAS. It did, however, find a violation in Pechstein's case, as CAS had refused her request for a public hearing in a dispute over a doping ban imposed by the International Skating Union; the court also held that her acceptance of CAS arbitration had been forced, since refusing it would have ended her ability to earn a living in her sport. Two judges dissented on the question of CAS's independence and impartiality. The sports law scholar Antoine Duval of the Asser Institute described the ruling as a "pyrrhic victory for the status quo at the CAS", arguing that it subjected CAS to Article 6 while wrongly finding it independent of sports governing bodies. For example, the ECHR found CAS and the Federal Supreme Court discriminated against and violated the privacy of runner Caster Semenya.

German speed skater Claudia Pechstein, who was unsuccessful in lifting a doping-related suspension in her CAS case, appealed to the Federal Court of Justice of Germany, which, however, ruled against her, recognising a lack of jurisdiction to revisit her case. The Federal Court ruled that CAS met the requirements of a court of arbitration according to German law and that CAS's independence from the parties was secured by the method of selecting arbitrators and the possibility to appeal to the Swiss Federal Tribunal. However, this decision was in turn overturned by the Federal Constitutional Court of Germany, which ordered a re-trial.

Proceedings before the CAS require payment of fees. As of 2025, appellants pay a fee of 1,000 CHF when filing. On accepting a case, CAS sets a fee as an advance on arbitration costs, normally paid in equal shares by the parties. If the advance is not paid, proceedings are terminated. The advance may be several tens of thousands of Swiss francs.

With the intermixing of sports and politics, the body was originally conceived by International Olympic Committee (IOC) president Juan Antonio Samaranch to deal with disputes arising during the Olympics. It was established as part of the IOC in 1984.

In 1992, the case of Gundel v. La Fédération Equestre Internationale was decided by the CAS, and then appealed to the Federal Supreme Court of Switzerland, challenging CAS impartiality. The Swiss court ruled that the CAS was a true court of arbitration but drew attention to the numerous links between the CAS and the IOC.

In response, the CAS underwent reforms to make itself more independent of the IOC, both organizationally and financially. The most significant change resulting from this reform was the creation of an "International Council of Arbitration for Sport" (ICAS) to look after the running and financing of the CAS, thereby taking the place of the IOC.

As of 2022, 9,695 cases had been submitted to CAS since 1986. Ordinary and ad hoc cases were first accepted in 1995, mediation cases in 1999, and anti-doping cases in 2016. As of August 2024, there are 422 CAS Arbitrators around the world, with 216 from Europe, and 52 Mediators.

In March 2011, CAS decided its first case on athlete biological passports (ABP) when it suspended two Italian cyclists, Franco Pellizotti and Pietro Caucchioli, for two years based on evidence from their blood profiles.

articles.title: Riemann hypothesis
paragraphs: In mathematics, the Riemann hypothesis is a theorem that states the Riemann zeta function has its zeros only at the negative even integers and at complex numbers with real part 12. First posed in 1859 by Bernhard Riemann, pure mathematicians consider the hypothesis to be one of the most important problems in the field. It is important in number theory because it implies bounds on the distribution of prime numbers. The name is also used for some closely related analogues such as the Riemann hypothesis for curves over finite fields, which was proved by André Weil around 1940.

The Riemann zeta function ζ is a function whose argument may be any complex number other than 1, and whose values are also complex. It has zeros at the negative even integers, called trivial zeros, and all other zeros are nontrivial zeros. The Riemann hypothesis is concerned with the locations of these nontrivial zeros, and states that all the nontrivial zeros lie on the critical line, consisting of the complex numbers 12+it where t is a real number and i is the imaginary unit.

The implications of the hypothesis and its generalizations extend across mathematics. The standard hypothesis establishes essentially the tightest possible bound for the error of the logarithmic integral in estimating the number of primes less than a specific value. Some conditional proofs assume the truth of generalizations of the hypothesis, such as those for Goldbach's weak conjecture—before it was proved unconditionally—and for Artin's conjecture on primitive roots. The Riemann hypothesis makes up part of Hilbert's eighth problem and is one of the Millennium Prize Problems of the Clay Mathematics Institute. The problem attracted numerous attempted proofs.

In November 2026, mathematician Levent Alpöge announced a formal proof of the Riemann hypothesis and its generalization to Dirichlet L-functions, developed with the assistance of the artificial intelligence model Claude. The proof, formalized in the proof assistant software Lean, was accepted by the Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative. A natural language proof has not been published as of 26 November 2026.

But the eta function series on the right converges not just when the real part of s is greater than one, but more generally whenever s has positive real part. Thus, the zeta function can be redefined as η(s)/(1−2/2s), extending it from Re⁡(s)>1 to the larger domain Re⁡(s)>0, except for the points where 1−2/2s is zero. These are the points s=1+2πin/log⁡2, where n can be any nonzero integer; the zeta function can be extended to these values too by taking limits (see the article on the Dirichlet eta function), giving a finite value for all values of s with positive real part except the simple pole at s=1.

One may then define ζ(s) for all remaining nonzero complex numbers s (Re⁡(s)≤0 and s≠0) by applying this equation outside the strip, and letting ζ(s) equal the right side of the equation whenever s has non-positive real part (and s≠0).

If s is a negative even integer, then ζ(s)=0, because the factor sin⁡(πs/2) vanishes; these are the zeta function's trivial zeros. (If s is a positive even integer this argument does not apply because the zeros of the sine function are canceled by the poles of the gamma function as it takes negative integer arguments.)

The value ζ(0)=−1/2 is not determined by the functional equation, but is the limiting value of ζ(s) as s approaches zero. The functional equation also implies that the zeta function has no zeros with negative real part other than the trivial zeros, so all nontrivial zeros lie in the critical strip where s has real part between 0 and 1.

The terms li⁡(xρ) involving the zeros of the zeta function need some care in their definition as li has branch points at 0 and 1, and are defined (for x>1) by analytic continuation in the complex variable ρ in the region Re⁡(ρ)>0; i.e., they should be considered as Ei(ρ log x). The other terms also correspond to zeros: the dominant term li⁡(x) comes from the pole at s=1, considered as a zero of multiplicity −1, and the remaining small terms come from the trivial zeros. For some graphs of the sums of the first few terms of this series see Riesel & Göhl (1970) or Zagier (1977).

This formula says that the zeros of the Riemann zeta function control the oscillations of primes around their "expected" positions. Riemann knew that the non-trivial zeros of the zeta function were symmetrically distributed about the line s=1/2+it, and he knew that all of its non-trivial zeros must lie in the range 0≤Re⁡(s)≤1. He checked that a few of the zeros lay on the critical line with real part 1/2 and suggested that they all do; this is the Riemann hypothesis.

The result has caught the imagination of most mathematicians because it is so unexpected, connecting two seemingly unrelated areas in mathematics; namely, number theory, which is the study of the discrete, and complex analysis, which deals with continuous processes.

On 20 November 2026, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at the AI company Anthropic, posted a formal proof of the hypothesis. He had used Claude, a large language model developed by Anthropic, to investigate the generalized Riemann hypothesis (GRH). He released a formalization in Lean, consisting of about 17 million lines of code. Development of the Lean proof spanned from 6 October to 16 November.

articles.title: ‘Strict liability’: The legal standard that could help rein in AI
paragraphs: Some people have begun using the legal system to rein in AI companies and the harms they are creating. Cases are mounting.

In October 2026, the parents of Bowen Wan sued OpenAI, charging that it’s ChatGPT agent may have instructed their daughter to stop taking her medication, leading to her death . In 2024, a mother sued the Character.AI company, claiming that its chatbot’s interactions with her son contributed to his suicide . The state of Kentucky later filed suit, claiming that Character.AI’s software exposed minors to self-harm and psychological manipulation.
Social media companies, powered by artificial intelligence, are also facing lawsuits about injuries they purportedly caused.
Regulating AI was a hot issue during the 2026 midterms, too. Several candidates who won their races have a regulation agenda .
I am a former litigator and a professor of business law, and all this action signals to me that people are looking to the law to protect them from AI harm.

But what is the legal liability of AI software? An answer may be found in a principle known as strict liability . Applied properly, strict liability could restrain the risky parts of the AI industry and still allow it to provide the tools the public wants.

Tort law protects people from negligence, such as who is responsible if you slip and fall in a store . Strict liability is part of tort law, but it is used to hold a person or company responsible for harm even if they were not at fault, not negligent or had no intent of creating trouble.

Two types of strict liability matter for AI. One addresses abnormally dangerous activity, such as blasting with dynamite or transporting radioactive material. The other addresses when a product hurts someone using it .

AI programs likely fit the abnormally dangerous standard. The touchstone case was tried in the U.K. in 1868. In the decision, the court stated that if someone has “anything” under their power that is “likely to do mischief if it escapes, [he] must keep it in at his peril” and is “answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape.” The defendant is liable even if they used “ the utmost care to prevent the harm .”

An attorney could pursue this avenue if a company builds AI software that is supposed to stay in a sandbox – a place isolated from the rest of a computer or network – but loses control of it . The AI industry’s recent admissions that the software creates all sorts of risks would make such cases stronger. When Anthropic filed for its initial public offering in October, numerous pages of the document detailed extraordinary risks that its frontier AI models could pose.

One hitch in applying this type of strict liability is that an activity must not be in common usage . Lawyers could make a strong case against so-called rogue AI that runs wild and isn’t available to most people.

Applying the danger standard could still fail to rein in AI companies or reward victims appropriately. In 1929, aviation was seen as abnormally dangerous . But damages were capped at US$8,300, which was not a large deterrent.

Attitudes changed in 1999, when the Montreal Convention standardized strict liability rules for international flights worldwide. It raised statutory damages and eliminated caps for negligence claims. Perhaps the most powerful tool in aviation liability today is for an authority to ground a company’s aircraft, which happened to Boeing after two fatal crashes with its 737 MAX planes.

Strict product liability is the other strategy for holding AI companies responsible for harm. In years past, courts tended to not see software as a product because it is intangible. But that view is shifting . In recent lawsuits alleging that social media hurt people, courts did see social media as a product and concluded that strict liability was applicable . Cases against Facebook have fallen into this category.

Character.AI’s recent bankruptcy filing came in part because of a lawsuit in which the court treated the software as a product . “ Design defects ” is the part of the doctrine gaining traction. To use this, a plaintiff shows that the product posed a foreseeable risk to someone using it. So far, the doctrine has worked when applied to the lack of guardrails in chatbots.

Pursuing strict liability could still run into snags. A court might order that AI software be turned off, or “grounded,” until it is improved. But as AI software creeps closer to being an operating system and is evermore embedded in everyone’s daily activities, it becomes difficult to suspend its use.

AI software by its nature is constantly “learning” and therefore changing. It is impossible for a company to promise that AI software will absolutely behave a certain way . In many cases, AI software is inherently incapable of supporting a guarantee about design safety. Still, strict liability is a way to hold the maker responsible, “even when those products evolve in ways not specifically desired or foreseeable by their manufacturers,” according to a Brookings Institution report.

I believe that if people are going to accept AI software as a boon to society, tough rules and sharp deterrents are needed. A strict liability system would shift risk from society to the companies seeking vast revenues.

The next steps will be sorting out whether to treat all or some AI software as a product, and whether the technology is ultrahazardous. If it is treated as that dangerous, AI can develop with incentives to reduce harms and ensure that people injured are compensated.
Deven Desai owns shares in Google, Inc. He received unrestricted research gifts from Google, Inc. and Facebook, Inc. a decade ago. He has not been employed by Google since 2010.

articles.title: Students creating documentaries with scientists deepens STEM belonging and public trust in science
paragraphs: Marine scientists navigate autonomous glider robots across the Atlantic Ocean and along the West Antarctic Peninsula, collecting data to help predict storm intensity.
When farmers’ fields are destroyed by an unknown pathogen, plant scientists spend years breeding new varieties of disease-resistant food crops.
A team of microbiologists explore deep-sea volcanoes in search of organisms that may contain anticancer compounds.

These are passionate people who are dedicated to seeking solutions to real-world problems. They are also the main characters in science documentaries produced in the Rutgers Immersive Learning Science Storytelling Lab that I oversee. Our lab pairs students with working scientists to co-create documentaries about research as it happens, while earning experiential learning credit.
At a time when confidence in science is declining, I was approached by scientists who wanted their authentic research stories communicated to broad audiences.

I am an educator, a researcher and anthropologist, and a science filmmaker who has been making science documentaries with Rutgers students and researchers since 2008. The science-in-action storytelling model I developed is intended to make the human journey of science visible to the public. Our stories communicate the process, motivations and integrity behind science, which helps earn public confidence and trust in science .

I also partner with STEM learning researchers to gauge whether our documentaries increase the relatability of scientists, increase public understanding of scientific processes and help students find belonging in STEM.
Science-in-action storytelling is composed of five steps that support student-scientist relationships.
First, the storytellers develop trust with the participating university scientists. This trust stems from shared respect and a mutual understanding of the co-creation process.
The scientists then invite storytellers into their labs and field sites, where we capture their research processes in real time. This is Step 2.

Our professional storytelling team, which includes students, then documents scientists conducting research, including experiments and data collection, as they describe the why and how of their work. Depending on the complexity of the project, we collect dozens to hundreds of hours of science-in-action video footage.

Importantly, this video data is maintained in our storytelling lab, as it often includes recordings of federally funded research. Maintaining the video data repository is a key component to establishing and sustaining trust with the participating scientists.

Step 3 invites students to immerse themselves in the video data and begin shaping the footage into documentary scenes, constructed using only the scientists’ words, without narration. As they analyze hours of footage, our students learn about the authentic scientific processes; in doing so, they participate in research through the process of storytelling.
Our students are not graded on their documentary skills, nor are they required to make a film. Instead, they are graded on the science they learn through the storytelling process.

Step 4 requires that the students share drafts of their documentary scenes with the featured scientist to verify the accuracy of the science communicated. This step is part of the foundational trust agreement with the scientists but is also an opportunity for the students to personally connect with scientists.

For Step 5, our lab works to distribute the documentaries to a wide variety of audiences, including the general public. Here we partner with STEM learning experts to assess audiences’ understanding of and trust in the science communicated in the film and audience perceptions of the featured scientists.

Our completed science-in-action documentaries have reached audiences far beyond the university. Our National Science Foundation-funded “ Antarctic Edge: 70° South ” had a theatrical release and aired on Netflix. “ Atlantic Crossing ” was broadcast on PBS stations and was included in a three-year Smithsonian exhibit . “ Fields of Devotion ” was shared by the Association of American Universities as part of its campaign to increase public trust in science . And our lab’s newest long-form documentary, “ Mysteries of 9° North,” co-created with 14 undergraduates and featuring scientists studying life at deep-sea volcanoes, will be released to the public in early 2027.

Our surveys capture how these science documentaries change audience understanding of science and how it is done. For example, after screening “ Antarctic Edge,” viewers’ self-reported understanding of climate change rose from 71% to 91% . On a 15-item knowledge quiz, average scores rose, with gains of up to 24 percentage points on the concepts they knew least about.

When 102 undergraduates were asked what made the scientists in “ Fields of Devotion ” relatable, they named passion for the subject (72%), desire to help others (71%) and commitment to their work (70%).

Our survey results also suggest that students who participated in the lab gained confidence and feelings of belonging in a science community. Undergraduates who once said they did not feel “smart enough” reported that they could now see themselves as scientists . All participating students reported that their collaboration with scientists positively transformed their understanding of science.
Nonscience majors gained a deep understanding of the scientific process, while science majors gained rare access to research outside their own disciplines.

Student-directed science documentaries include “ Growing the Caribbean Glider Fleet,” featuring scientists monitoring hurricane development; “ Biting Back: The Lifesaving Potential of Catnip,” about the development of natural insect repellents; “ Where Waters Meet on the Breathing Shore,” featuring climate scientists studying coastal ecosystems; “ The B.A.S.I.L Project,” about USDA-funded plant-breeding research; “ Ocean Farming,” about NOAA supported oyster breeding; “ The Women of Nsongwe,” about USAID-supported agriculture projects in Zambia; and “ Skycatcher,” about an NSF-funded atmospheric chemistry study in Alabama.

This science-in-action model offers a path forward that other universities could follow. Institutions can strengthen students’ STEM learning and science identities while training a new generation of credible, relatable voices for science.

articles.title: Fires Char New Guinea
paragraphs: New Guinea, the world’s second-largest island, harbors an extraordinary variety of plant life across more than a dozen distinct ecoregions, including seasonally dry savannas, tropical rainforests, and lowland swamp forests. But in September and October 2026, as drought gripped New Guinea (sometimes called Papua) amid a strong El Niño, fires scorched the island and smoke shrouded large swaths of it for weeks.

The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-20 satellite captured this image of thick smoke streaming from the southern part of the island on October 11, 2026. In recent weeks, soaring levels of air pollution delayed and canceled flights, closed schools, and prompted officials in some areas to urge children and older people to wear masks.

“Sometimes smoke that has drifted into the convection of nearby thunderstorms will get washed out or lofted up into the upper troposphere, but a lot of smoke stays near the surface and causes air quality problems,” said Robert Field, an associate research scientist at NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies and Columbia University. “It’s a horrible situation.”

According to the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED), a fire emissions monitoring system, fires in Papua New Guinea, on the eastern half of the island, had released nearly 32 megatons of carbon by October 17, more than any other year on record at that point in the year (charts above). “Emissions are already much higher than the 2015 total for the year, and it’s very likely that this will become the highest year on record for Papua New Guinea, even surpassing 1997,” said Guido van der Werf, a fire scientist at Wageningen University & Research.

On the Indonesian side, sometimes called West New Guinea or Indonesian Papua, carbon emissions exceeded 35 megatons, the third highest after 2015 and 1997, other El Niño years with severe fires. Van der Werf led the development of GFED, a satellite-driven modeling framework that uses a mix of remote sensing, vegetation characteristics, and other information to estimate the extent of vegetation fires and the emissions over nearly three decades.

Unusually dry weather—a byproduct of El Niño shifting rainfall patterns —has primed ecosystems across the island to burn. The southernmost part of Papua New Guinea, dominated by relatively fire-prone savannas and grasslands of the Trans-Fly region, went more than 90 consecutive days without rain, according to Papua New Guinea’s National Weather Service . Since August, parts of the region have seen precipitation of roughly 5 to 10 percent of normal, according to the weather service’s data. Local news outlets report that drought is causing crop failures, water shortages, and school disruptions .

In this normally wet part of the world, people ignite the vast majority of fires, researchers say. Crop fires, pasture maintenance, deforestation and land clearing, and hunting are all common reasons people burn in New Guinea. In dry conditions, managed fires sometimes spread and burn uncontrolled as wildfires, particularly in the drier, southernmost parts of the island.

“We’re seeing an exceptionally high level of fire activity in Papua New Guinea and Eastern Indonesia, particularly Indonesian Papua and Kalimantan, this year compared with Sumatra and other parts of Western Indonesia,” said Yang Chen, an associate researcher at the University of California, Irvine. “Papua has emerged as Indonesia’s new deforestation frontier.”

Over the past two decades, land in Indonesian Papua has been cleared for industrial oil palm and pulpwood plantations, shifting small-scale cultivation, urban expansion, and mining . According to Global Forest Watch, the region lost 27,000 hectares of primary forest in 2025, nearly double the 2024 total and the most since 2017.

Sumatra’s fires are relatively low compared to other drought years partly because many areas are already developed. “Areas with large oil palm, sugarcane, or pulpwood plantations also often have their own private fire brigades to protect their assets,” said Field. “It’s in unmanaged areas or primary forest edges where we’re generally seeing the most fire.”
Researchers expect the fires to continue until the heavy rains of the wet season arrive in the southern part of New Guinea, typically in early November.

articles.title: Your gut bacteria helps your body keep track of time, and when you eat influences how much nutrition you get from food
paragraphs: How your body processes food is significantly influenced by daily rhythms tied to 24-hour light-dark cycles. In new research published in the scientific journal Cell Host & Microbe, my colleagues and I found that the microbes living in your gut are the hidden timekeepers behind this system.

Gut microbes convert dietary signals into molecules that intestinal cells use to synchronize nutrient absorption with feeding times. In mice, this microbe-controlled timing mechanism maximizes the nutrients the mouse’s body takes in and supports growth, especially when food is scarce.
When mice consumed an excess of calories, however, that same system fueled obesity .

Because of Earth’s rotation, all animals – including humans – experience rhythmic shifts of day and night . Your eyes and brain use light signals to coordinate your body’s activities with environmental changes and nutrient availability. Disruption of this temporal alignment, such as through jet lag and night-shift work, is associated with a range of health disorders .

However, light is not the only timekeeper. Your intestines are home to trillions of microbes, called the gut microbiome . They play a key role in shaping your physiology, such as metabolism, immunity and even brain activity.

Intriguingly, the microbiome also influences the daily biological rhythms of hosts . My colleagues and I had previously shown that depleting gut bacteria in mice weakens circadian rhythms in the small intestine and alters them in the colon . These disruptions can affect how well your intestine absorbs and processes fats and other lipids, which may contribute to metabolic disorders such as obesity.
But if gut microbes are never exposed to the light, how do they track time? New research from my team suggests that the answer is feeding time.

We found that the gut microbiota can metabolize phytate – a food component commonly found in grains, beans, nuts and seeds – and convert it into molecules that activate a specific protein in intestinal cells, subsequently turning on genes involved in transporting nutrients. Conversely, when fasting, a decrease in phytate levels leads to reduced microbial activity and a drop in nutrient absorption.
Through this pathway, microbes align intestinal absorption with when you typically eat, which maximizes the efficiency of nutrient absorption.
Our findings suggest that, like light, food provides time-of-day signals that gut microbes read to determine how your body functions.
People have co-evolved with their gut microbiota for millennia, implying this microbe-controlled time system carries benefits.

For most of human history, food was scarce . We hypothesized that this microbial pathway might help people survive and grow under starvation conditions. To test this idea, we fed mice a nutrient-poor diet and gave some of them either a common gut microbe or a molecule it produces that is linked to circadian regulation. We found that undernourished young mice who were given this bacterium or the microbial molecule grew taller and healthier than mice that weren’t, suggesting that this microbial pathway promotes growth and metabolic health when nutrients are limited.

However, many people today have constant access to abundant calories. Rather than nutrient scarcity, obesity has become the dominant dietary challenge. We found that for mice under high-calorie conditions, this microbial pathway promotes excess fat uptake in the body and worsens diet-induced obesity.

Therefore, the same gut microbiome mechanism that helped people thrive can become a liability when it encounters an environment it was never designed for. This is an example of evolutionary mismatch .

articles.title: 1999 New Zealand general election
paragraphs: The 1999 New Zealand general election was held on 27 November 1999 to determine the composition of the 46th New Zealand Parliament. The governing National Party, led by Prime Minister Jenny Shipley, was defeated, being replaced by a coalition of Helen Clark's Labour Party and the smaller Alliance. This marked an end to nine years of the Fourth National Government, and the beginning of the Fifth Labour Government which would govern for nine years in turn, until its loss to the National Party in the 2008 general election. It was the first New Zealand election where both major parties had female leaders.

Before the election, the National Party had an unstable hold on power. After the 1996 election National had formed a coalition with the populist New Zealand First party and its controversial leader, Winston Peters. The coalition was unpopular, as New Zealand First was seen as opposed to the National government, and had made many statements in the 1996 election campaign to that effect, such as saying that only through New Zealand First could National Party be toppled, and Peters said that he would not accept Jim Bolger as prime minister, Bill Birch as Finance Minister or Jenny Shipley in a social welfare portfolio. NZ First's support crashed, though this was also partly caused by scandals and by mid-1997, NZ First was polling at as low as 2%. National also polled badly, and Jim Bolger was replaced as prime minister with Jenny Shipley.

Gradually, however, the relationship between the two parties deteriorated, and Peters took his party out of the coalition, after Shipley sacked him from her cabinet. A number of New Zealand First MPs deserted Peters, establishing themselves as independents or as members of newly established parties. By forming agreements with these MPs, National was able to keep itself in office, but its control was often unsteady. The polls were still initially close, but without NZ First support, National's chances of forming a government were slim. Eventually, Labour Party gained a solid lead over National.

The Labour Party, which had been in Opposition since losing the 1990 election, presented a strong challenge, particularly due to its agreement with the smaller Alliance party. The two had not previously enjoyed good relations, primarily due to the presence of the NewLabour Party as one of the Alliance's key members. NewLabour had been established by Jim Anderton, a former Labour MP who quit the party in protest over the economic reforms of Roger Douglas, which were often blamed for Labour's election loss in 1990. Gradually, as the Labour Party withdrew from Rogernomics, the Alliance (led by Anderton) reduced its hostility towards Labour, but it was not until shortly before the 1999 election that a formal understanding was reached regarding a possible left-wing coalition. This agreement was deemed a necessary step towards building a credible alternative to the National Party.
This election was the first one in New Zealand's history where both main parties were led by women, being repeated again in the 2020 election.
Fifteen MPs intended to retire at the end of the 45th Parliament.
The Greens had contested the election under the Alliance banner, but split from the Alliance in 1997, remaining in their parliamentary faction.

The election took place on 27 November. Less than 84.1% of the 2,509,365 people registered to vote turned out for the election. This was the lowest turnout for some time, although it would drop further in the 2002 election. A total of 679 candidates stood for electorate seats, representing 36 parties. Party lists comprised 760 candidates from 22 parties. The new government was sworn in on 10 December.

In the election 965 candidates stood, and there were 22 registered parties with party lists. Of the candidates, 482 were electorate and list, 197 were electorate only, and 286 were list only. 67% of candidates (647) were male and 33% (318) female.

Labour Party won 49 seats in parliament. When combined with the ten seats won by the Alliance, the coalition was two seats short of an absolute majority. It was able to form a new government with support from the Green Party, which entered parliament for the first time as an independent party (having previously been a part of the Alliance). The Green Party's entry to parliament was by a narrow margin, however – in order to gain seats, it needed to either win 5% of the party vote or win an electorate seat, neither of which the party appeared likely to do. Helen Clark openly encouraged Labour supporters in the Coromandel to give their constituency vote to Green Party co-leader Jeanette Fitzsimons and their party vote to Labour. However, when all special votes (that is, votes cast by people who were not able to attend a polling place in their electorate on the day of the election) were counted, the Greens had narrowly reached not one but both targets – Jeanette Fitzsimons won the electorate of Coromandel by 250 votes, and the party gained 5.16% of the vote.

The National Party, while not performing exceptionally poorly, failed to gain enough support to keep it in power. It won 39 seats, ten fewer than the Labour Party. ACT New Zealand, a potential coalition partner for National, gained nine seats. While this was an increase on ACT's previous election results, it was not sufficient to enable the National Party to form a government. National's former coalition partner, New Zealand First, performed poorly, with voters punishing it for the problems in the last government. The party received less than 5% of the vote, and so would have been removed from parliament had Winston Peters not retained his electorate of Tauranga, something he did by only 63 votes. None of the MPs who deserted New Zealand First were returned to parliament.

articles.title: 1909 Chinese provincial elections
paragraphs: The Qing dynasty held its first set of provincial assembly elections from February to June 1909. Following a lengthy period of political turmoil which included the failure of the 1898 Hundred Days' Reform and the 1899–1901 Boxer Rebellion, the constitutionalist movement gained approval from the imperial court and Empress Dowager Cixi. Seeing local self-governance as a first step towards constitutionalism, in 1907 the Qing Government approved the creation of provincial assemblies. The following year, an indirect election system was outlined to fill these assemblies. They were held in 21 of the country's 22 provinces; Xinjiang elections were postponed due to low rates of literacy in Chinese. Suffrage and candidacy was limited to a small population of wealthy men, most of whom were members of the scholar-gentry. Public attitudes towards the elections were generally apathetic, and corruption, fraud, and vote buying were common across the country. Turnout greatly varied between provinces and regions, but was generally low.

The elected provincial assemblies were composed largely of constitutionalists, who were often divided between progressive and conservative wings. Some assemblymen were clandestine members of the revolutionary organization Tongmenghui. The assemblies agitated for a variety of economic and political reforms, which brought them into conflict with the provincial governors, who held veto power over the bodies. The assemblies participated in parliamentary elections, electing half of the members of the National Assembly. Before another set of elections could be held, the Qing dynasty collapsed in the 1911 Revolution and the Republic of China was founded. The first provincial elections under the new government were held in 1912.

Since the Song dynasty (960–1279), scholars were appointed to positions in the imperial Chinese bureaucracy through the imperial examination system. This system was carried through to the late Qing dynasty, although it had come under increasing intellectual opposition during the late 19th century as corrupt and ineffective. As it entered the 20th century, the Qing empire was in social and political turmoil, facing a series of defeats by the Western powers. Despite the repression of the Hundred Days' Reform in 1898, the constitutionalist movement continued to advocate for the creation of a constitutional government in lieu of Qing absolutism. The writer Liang Qichao emerged as the movement's most influential leader.

The de facto head of state Empress Dowager Cixi, previously opposed to the reform movement, had begun to grow sympathetic in the wake of China's humiliation in the Boxer Rebellion and the upset victory of the constitutionalist Empire of Japan in the Russo-Japanese War. The administrative, bureaucratic, and judicial systems were the first major targets for reform; redundant and archaic offices were abolished, the functions of the Six Boards (powerful imperial government agencies) were transferred to a new set of civil ministries, and the three northeastern provinces were integrated into the administrative framework of the other provinces. In June 1905, prominent imperial officials Yuan Shikai, Zhang Zhidong, and Zhou Fu jointly submitted a call for the creation of a constitutional monarchy.

The Qing government reduced the frequency of the imperial exams and began to promote a Western-style education system; when this met resistance by local gentry, the examination system was abolished in 1905. The government initially intended to replace the imperial examinations with a new form of civil service exam; however, little progress was made in its creation. Instead, the central government began to pursue elections as an alternative to examinations. Although new entries into the gentry ended with the examination system, the class still held immense influence. Including their family members, slightly under two percent of the population were members of the gentry by the late 19th century. Although the majority had reached this status through the examination system, an increasing number had purchased gentry status from the central government, at a cost which had been dramatically lowered in the decades following the Taiping Rebellion.

Proposals for local and provincial assemblies were raised following the end of the Hundred Days' Reform. In the first few years of the 1900s, reformist and revolutionary thinkers such as Sun Yat-sen, Ho Kai, and Kang Youwei began to advocate for such assemblies, citing both Western systems of local government and the traditional governance system of fengjian. As the central government began to embrace the constitutional movement, reformist officials began to advocate for the establishment of local self-governance as a preliminary step towards a constitutional government.

Upon the recommendation of a 1906 state committee headed by Prince Zaifeng, Cixi issued an edict in support of a constitution and national legislature. The next year, the Grand Council established the Constitutional Commission to begin a twelve-year constitutional reform process, inspired by the Japanese Meiji Restoration and constitution. Under the supervision of Yuan Shikai, the Tianjin County Council held the first Western-style elections in Chinese history in August 1907. Following a proposal by Yuan in July, on 19 October, the Constitutional Commission received imperial assent to organize provincial assemblies (諮議局; Zīyìjú), in preparation for the establishment of the National Assembly (資政院; Zīzhèngyuàn) and proper provincial legislatures. Following this, various provinces (including Jiangsu, Guangdong, Guangxi, and Fengtian) created unelected provincial assemblies with appointees from the local gentry.

In July 1908, the central court produced regulations for the implementation of provincial assemblies and their elections. The "Regulations for Provincial Assembly Elections" was a 115-clause document which established the electoral processes. The provincial assembly elections were indirect elections via an electoral college; voters would vote on a slate of electors, who would in turn elect the provincial assemblymen. In addition to their provincial duties, these assemblymen would elect the members of the National Assembly in a separate election later in the year.

Only men were allowed to participate in the election. Both voters and elector candidates were subject to the same set of requirements, beyond a minimum age of 25 for voters and 30 for electors. Eligible men were required to have either taught at above the primary level for at least three years, graduated from a secondary school, held the imperial examination rank of gongsheng (貢生) or higher, held a post at or above the seventh rank of the civil service or the fifth rank of the military, or had wealth (either through a business or land holdings) exceeding 5,000 yuan. Criminals, opium users, police officers, students, priests, and those with family members in disreputable careers were barred from voting or standing as candidates. If a voter was not native to their province, they were required to have resided there for over ten years, and have wealth exceeding 10,000 yuan. These regulations resulted in the overwhelming majority of the population being ineligible to vote.

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis are bringing their war to Saudi Arabia – and reframing the narrative of being an Iranian proxy
paragraphs: A deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh’s international airport has highlighted how the Yemeni group is reframing its perceived “Iran proxy” role and shifting its regional focus to its ongoing battle against Saudi Arabia. The Oct. 10 strike, in which 13 people were killed and hundreds injured, was the most violent episode on Saudi Arabian soil since the beginning of the war in Iran in February.
It was followed by further – albeit less deadly – missile barrages in the days since. The violence, moreover, comes just as the kingdom is hosting a major conference for oil producers.

As a longtime analyst of Yemeni politics, I see the latest attacks as another illustration of both the expanding regional stalemate across the Middle East and the need to understand how Yemen’s decade-long war is having effects far beyond its territory.

The Houthi movement first emerged as a militarized political actor in Yemen in 2004 and has been locked in a multiyear civil war against the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed central government. Currently, the Houthis control about a third of the territory and two-thirds of the population. They are undoubtedly Yemen’s most powerful armed force, despite lacking access to warplanes, and have developed an arsenal of long-range missiles and drones.
All along, the Houthis have frequently been portrayed by their adversaries and many external observers as a proxy for Iran, the chief regional rival to Saudi Arabia.

It’s true that the movement has long been broadly aligned with Tehran and frequently shared regional objections, even if the relationship is complex and varied . At the same time, the evolution of the Houthi movement remains intimately connected to Yemen’s domestic political context and to a historical feud specific to the country – something I and many other scholars have researched.

What is particularly significant in the current context of an escalating fight with Saudi Arabia, however, is the way in which the Houthi leadership has sought to reframe its military engagement over the course of 2026 so that it does not appear to be directed by Iran.
This shift is analytically important because it reveals how Houthi leaders understand the political effectiveness of particular narratives and how they seek to legitimize their actions.

When the United States and Israel launched their attack on Iran on Feb. 28, many observers expected the Houthis to enter the conflict swiftly. Their previous intervention in the Red Sea – between November 2023 and May 2025 – in support of Palestinians after Israel’s war in Gaza had, to some extent, provided a blueprint for disrupting maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

The symbolic returns of their earlier campaign had been considerable. On the one hand, it demonstrated the Houthis’ willingness to act in support of Gaza at a time when many Arab governments were widely perceived as turning their backs on the plight of Palestinians. It also revealed the movement’s capacity to disrupt global supply chains and affect international trade far beyond Yemen.

But the Houthis remained on the sidelines for several months after the initial U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Their leaders appeared to disregard reports that Iranian decision-makers had called on them, in July 2026, to close the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb to maritime traffic.

Assuming that the Houthis would automatically act at Tehran’s command reflected a misreading of Yemeni history and of the identity markers that shape the movement’s political legitimacy. Acting in support of Palestinians could be framed for a domestic and regional audience as an expression of Arab solidarity. But acting on behalf of Iran, a non-Arab Persian country composed almost entirely of Twelver Shia Muslims, was considerably more difficult to rationalize in Arab Yemen where Twelver Shia Muslims are absent and Sunnis are the majority.
The Houthis’ reentry into the regional conflict in August took place alongside a shift in their political narrative, which increasingly centered on their long-standing adversary, Saudi Arabia.

Although the strategic consequences of their actions may ultimately benefit Iran in its own regional and international conflicts, the Houthis see their military campaign against Saudi Arabia chiefly as an act of national defense.

During the summer of 2026, an important episode went largely unnoticed in the Western media: the Houthis’ attempt to establish the reopening of Sanaa International Airport through the surprise departure of a Tehran-bound flight and its subsequent return.

The airport, located in the Houthi-controlled capital, had been closed since late 2024 following Israeli strikes . Its continued closure meant that access to and exit from Houthi-controlled territory remained subject to restrictions imposed by the movement’s adversaries. These included the authorities controlling Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognized government.

From the Houthis’ perspective, their sovereignty consequently remained incomplete. The airport’s closure not only restricted civilian movement but also limited their ability to send supporters abroad for training and potentially to receive military equipment. On July 13, the Saudi military’s subsequent bombing of the Sanaa runway, as the incoming aircraft from Tehran approached, provided the movement an opportunity to reignite its confrontation with Riyadh.

After more than three years of a de facto ceasefire and difficult negotiations, Riyadh appeared, as in its dealings with Iran, increasingly eager to extricate itself from the region’s protracted conflicts. Sensing an opening, the Houthi leadership responded by invoking a logic of tit-for-tat retaliation.

The Houthis’ tactics today are a kind of mirror to the 2015 launch of a Saudi-led bombing campaign and blockade of the Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen that has led to years of protracted civil war. The Houthis now claim the right to impose reciprocal restrictions on Saudi Arabia, particularly by targeting its ports and oil-exporting infrastructure.

The Houthis’ new tactic serves two purposes. First, it allows the Houthis to redirect responsibility for the economic and humanitarian crisis in and around Sanaa toward the Saudi-enforced blockade rather than their own governance failures, mismanagement and corruption. Second, it provides a rationale for escalating the conflict across the region.

Previously, the Houthi military leadership had halted attacks on Israeli-linked shipping in the Red Sea following the formal Gaza ceasefire of October 2025, despite having repeatedly come under bombardment. It had likewise suspended attacks on American vessels following an agreement with the Trump administration in May 2025.

These decisions demonstrated a degree of pragmatism beneath the movement’s inflammatory rhetoric. That pragmatism appeared to persist even as the Houthis resumed their regional military engagement, with American diplomats reportedly meeting Houthi representatives in Oman in September 2026.

articles.title: Song dynasty
paragraphs: The Song dynasty (SUUNG) was an imperial dynasty of China that ruled from 960 to 1279. The dynasty was founded by Emperor Taizu of Song, who usurped the throne of the Later Zhou dynasty and went on to conquer the rest of the Ten Kingdoms, ending the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. The Song often came into conflict with the contemporaneous Liao, Western Xia, and Jin dynasties in northern China. After retreating to southern China following attacks by the Jin dynasty, the Song was eventually conquered by the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty.

The dynasty's history is divided into two periods: during the Northern Song (北宋; 960–1127), the capital was in the northern city of Bianjing (now Kaifeng) and the dynasty controlled most of what is now East China. The Southern Song (南宋; 1127–1279) comprised the period following the loss of control over the northern half of Song territory to the Jurchen-led Jin dynasty in the Jin–Song wars. At that time, the Song court retreated south of the Yangtze and established its capital at Lin'an (now Hangzhou). Although the Song dynasty had lost control of the traditional Chinese heartlands around the Yellow River, the Southern Song Empire contained a large population and productive agricultural land, sustaining a robust economy. In 1234, the Jin dynasty was conquered by the Mongols, who took control of northern China, maintaining uneasy relations with the Southern Song. Möngke Khan, the fourth Great Khan of the Mongol Empire, died in 1259 while besieging the mountain castle Diaoyucheng in Chongqing. His younger brother Kublai Khan was proclaimed the new Great Khan and in 1271 founded the Yuan dynasty. After two decades of sporadic warfare, Kublai Khan's armies conquered the Song dynasty in 1279 after defeating the Southern Song in the Battle of Yamen, and reunited China under the Yuan dynasty.

Technology, science, philosophy, mathematics, and engineering flourished during the Song era. The Song dynasty was the first in world history to issue banknotes or true paper money and the first Chinese government to establish a permanent standing navy. This dynasty saw the first surviving records of the chemical formula for gunpowder, the invention of gunpowder weapons such as fire arrows, bombs, and the fire lance. It also saw the first discernment of true north using a compass, first recorded description of the pound lock, and improved designs of astronomical clocks. Economically, the Song dynasty was unparalleled with a gross domestic product three times larger than that of Europe during the 12th century. China's population doubled in size between the 10th and 11th centuries. This growth was made possible by expanded rice cultivation, use of early-ripening rice from Southeast and South Asia, and production of widespread food surpluses. The Northern Song census recorded 20 million households, double that of the Han and Tang dynasties. It is estimated that the Northern Song had a population of 90 million people. This dramatic increase of population fomented an economic revolution in pre-modern China.

The expansion of the population, growth of cities, and emergence of a national economy led to the gradual withdrawal of the central government from direct intervention in the economy. The lower gentry assumed a larger role in local administration and affairs. Song society was vibrant, and cities had lively entertainment quarters. Citizens gathered to view and trade artwork, and intermingled at festivals and in private clubs. The spread of literature and knowledge was enhanced by the rapid expansion of woodblock printing and the 11th-century invention of movable type printing. Philosophers such as Cheng Yi and Zhu Xi reinvigorated Confucianism with new commentary, infused with Buddhist ideals, and emphasized a new organization of classic texts that established the doctrine of Neo-Confucianism. Although civil service examinations had existed since the Sui dynasty, they became much more prominent in the Song period. Officials gaining power through imperial examination led to a shift from a military-aristocratic elite to a scholar-bureaucratic elite.

After usurping the throne of the Later Zhou dynasty, Emperor Taizu of Song (r. 960–976) spent sixteen years conquering the rest of China proper, reuniting much of the territory that had once belonged to the Han and Tang empires and ending the upheaval of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. In Kaifeng, he established a strong central government over the empire. The establishment of this capital marked the start of the Northern Song period. He ensured administrative stability by promoting the civil service examination system of drafting state bureaucrats by skill and merit (instead of aristocratic or military position) and promoted projects that ensured efficiency in communication throughout the empire. In one such project, cartographers created detailed maps of each province and city that were then collected in a large atlas. Emperor Taizu also promoted groundbreaking scientific and technological innovations by supporting works like the astronomical clock tower designed and built by the engineer Zhang Sixun.

The Song court maintained diplomatic relations with Chola India, the Fatimid Caliphate of Egypt, Srivijaya in modern-day Indonesia, the Kara-Khanid Khanate in Central Asia, the Goryeo Kingdom in Korea, Đại Cồ Việt and the Kingdom of Champa in Vietnam, and other countries that were also trade partners with Japan. Chinese records even mention an embassy from the ruler of "Fu lin" (拂菻, i.e. the Byzantine Empire), Michael VII Doukas, and its arrival in 1081. However, China's closest neighbouring states had the greatest impact on its domestic and foreign policy. From its inception under Taizu, the Song dynasty alternated between warfare and diplomacy with the ethnic Khitans of the Liao dynasty in the northeast and with the Tanguts of the Western Xia in the northwest. The Song dynasty used military force in an attempt to quell the Liao dynasty and to recapture the Sixteen Prefectures, a territory under Khitan control since 938 that was traditionally considered to be part of China proper (most parts of today's Beijing and Tianjin). Song forces were repulsed by the Liao forces, who engaged in aggressive yearly campaigns into Northern Song territory until 1005, when the signing of the Chanyuan Treaty ended these northern border clashes. The Song were forced to provide tribute to the Khitans, although this did little damage to the Song economy since the Khitans were economically dependent upon importing massive amounts of goods from the Song. More significantly, the Song state recognized the Liao state as its diplomatic equal. The Song created an extensive defensive forest along the Song–Liao border to thwart potential Khitan cavalry attacks.

articles.title: Seeking Refuge on Resolution Island
paragraphs: In the late 1800s, wildlife conservationists in New Zealand were recognizing how predators such as stoats, brought to the country to control other nonnative animal populations, were becoming a threat to native birds. Naturalists at the time surmised that some of the nation’s islands could serve as sanctuaries where endemic species could persist, free from the voracious newcomers.

Resolution Island, located in the Fiordland region along the rugged southwest edge of New Zealand’s South Island, was one of the first eyed for this purpose. Conservationist Thomas Henry Potts proposed in 1872 that the island could be a place where “wingless species, and birds of feeble powers of flight, might there find a refuge for some of their representatives.”

So began an early systematic effort to protect kiwi, kākāpō, and other native birds on Resolution Island, the largest of the approximately 90 islands in Fiordland National Park . This image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on December 12, 2025, shows the island’s setting amid a landscape of steep-sided valleys carved by glaciers and now inundated by the ocean.

The uninhabited island rises from sea level to the summit of Mount Clerke at 1,069 meters (3,507 feet). Its diverse habitats and vegetation communities range from bogs and wetlands near the coast to widespread podocarp forests at middle elevations to tussock grasslands in the subalpine and alpine areas. Offshore, the Taumoana (Five Fingers Peninsula) Marine Reserve protects estuarine and wave-exposed rocky reef habitats at the entrance to Dusky Sound, east of Five Fingers Peninsula.

Farther into the sound, Pigeon Island was the onetime home of Richard Henry, who was named caretaker of Resolution Island after it was designated a reserve in 1891. In what some have called a “ landmark effort,” Henry spent years transporting more than 700 birds, mostly kiwi and kākāpō, by rowboat to Resolution and other would-be island sanctuaries nearby.

In 1900, however, people began spotting mustelids on Resolution. It turns out the island is within swimming distance for animals such as stoats. Henry was intent on trapping the interlopers but eventually abandoned the project and moved on to caretaking work on another island. The spirit of his efforts lives on, though. A Department of Conservation program started in 2008 aims to control stoat populations and bolster native species on Resolution.
